title: Course Précis
text: Throughout the semester, you will work individually and as a collective to develop a synthetic overview of the key concepts of this course — a high-quality summary of the material that you can take with you when the semester ends. This is the course précis. It is the one assignment whose primary audience is your future self: done well, it is the document you will reach for years from now when you need to remember how the pieces of the development literature fit together. This page provides detailed instructions; the assignments page has the summary and the syllabus has grade weights and policies.

title: Course Précis
text:
What it is
The précis is a combination of words and figures. We will especially think about causal chains — what causes development, through what mechanisms, on what evidence — so your document must include these chains as diagrams, not only as prose. A reader should be able to look at your figures and see your understanding of how geography, institutions, states, markets, international forces, and household behavior connect to development outcomes, and where the major theories disagree about those connections.
There is no fixed page length. Most strong précis documents end up somewhere around 6–10 pages including figures, but I will evaluate synthesis, not volume. A tight document that maps the arguments accurately beats a long one that summarizes each book in sequence.

title: Course Précis
section: How it builds across the semester
text:
How it builds across the semester
The précis is not a document you write at the end; it is a document you revise all term. The course is structured to help you develop a habit of consistently revising and updating it:

Your session notes are the raw material. Every Part 1 entry states a reading’s central causal claim — those claims are the nodes and arrows of your map. The Connector role does précis work explicitly: each week, the Connector’s additions help revise and update the shared causal map we develop together in class, and that shared map informs (but does not replace) each student’s individual document. Therefore, everyone in the class will be better off if the Connector for the week takes their role seriously and shares their notes with the group. The Discussion Leaders should be sure to structure class conversation to ensure that there is ample discussion on connections across weeks. The better your session notes as well as the notes you take during class discussion, the easier time you’ll have constructing your course précis.
The Oct 5 workshop is the first checkpoint. Bring a working draft that maps the causal arguments of Sen, Koyama & Rubin, and Evans against each other. We will spend the session comparing maps, arguing about where the arrows go, and identifying what each framework treats as the binding constraint on development. Your draft can be rough — hand-drawn figures are welcome at this stage — but you must do the pre-work; the class session will not be helpful if you show up unprepared.
Each new book complicates the map. After the Africa book, A Thousand Cuts, Poor Economics, and the AI unit, expect to revise: some causal arrows will see their evidence strengthen, some causal pathways may seem to diminish, and some of what looked like settled understanding of what causes development in September will no longer seem so straightforward in November. Tracking those revisions is the intellectual point of the assignment.

title: Course Précis
Course Précis
text:
Evaluation
I evaluate the précis on the accuracy with which it represents the arguments we studied, the quality of the synthesis across books (connections and adjudication, not book-by-book summary), the clarity and correctness of the causal diagrams, and its usefulness as a standalone document — could a strong student entering this course next year learn the terrain from your précis? Figures may be drawn in any tool you like, or drawn by hand and scanned cleanly.

title: Course Précis
text:
Policies
The course generative AI policy applies: AI may assist with research and, heavily edited and revised, with writing — and all use must be disclosed in a brief AI-use note. Keep in mind what the précis is for: it is precisely your own synthesis that makes the document valuable, to you most of all, and a map you did not build yourself will not serve you when you reach for it later.

title: Session Notes & Discussion Roles
text: Session notes are the core way that students meaningfully prepare for each meeting of this seminar. Every member writes before every class that has assigned reading, everyone’s writing is used in the room, and each of you has a different job for discussion each week. This page provides detailed instructions for this set of assignments; the assignments page has the summary and the syllabus has grade weights and policies.

title: Session Notes & Discussion Roles
text:
The note
Bring five printed copies of your structured session notes to class — one for me, and one for each of you. Each note has two parts.

Part 1 — the core (200–300 words, everyone)
Answer three questions about the day’s reading:

The claim. What is the reading’s central causal claim about development? State it in your own words, as precisely as you can — what causes what, through what mechanism?
The evidence. What evidence does the author offer, and does it convince you? Name the kind of evidence (historical narrative, cross-country comparison, case study, experiment) and say where it is strongest and weakest.
Your argument. One point you are prepared to argue in class — a disagreement with the author, an extension, or a tension with something we read earlier.



Part 2 — your role (100–150 words)
Each week you hold one of four roles, and your note adds a short section written from that role’s perspective:


 Discussion Leader
Develop a set of 3–5 discussion questions that you think are most central to understanding and evaluating the reading. Good discussion questions move progressively from concrete to interpretive and from narrow to wide. Next to each question, provide a sentence on why this question matters. In class, you open the discussion and keep it moving — when a thread exhausts itself, you bring us to the next question. I, as the instructor, will help to keep the conversation moving productively and can assist students with decoding any questions that arise from the reading. Note that in many class sessions I will have a short set of slides to present to help ground the discussion in a clear narrative arc that is informed by the structure of international development as an academic discipline.


 Skeptic
Interrogate the evidence. Identify the weakest link in the causal chain: an alternative explanation the author hasn’t ruled out, a measurement or design problem, a case that doesn’t fit. In class, you make the strongest version of the counterargument — even if you personally find the author convincing.


 Connector
Tie the reading to the rest of the course. Where does it agree, conflict, or fill a gap relative to earlier books and articles? What would this author say to one we’ve already read? In class, you will bring in these comparisons — and your connections will help revise and update the shared causal map we will develop throughout the semester to inform each student’s course précis.


 Practitioner
Translate the argument into practice. If this author is right, what should a government, international organization, NGO, or firm do differently? What would the argument’s policy implications cost, and who would resist them? In class, you ground the discussion in application.

title: Session Notes & Discussion Roles
text:
Rotation
Roles are assigned in week 1 and rotate weekly, so you hold each role for a full week (both sessions) and cycle through all four roughly every four weeks — about three turns in each role across the semester. The rotation schedule is posted on Canvas alongside the Data Project 1 region sign-up sheet.

title: Session Notes & Discussion Roles
text:
How notes get used
We open most sessions with a short slide-based lecture from me. This will anchor our discussion to broader ideas, claims, and debates in the academic and practitioner community. Then, we will lay out the four Part 1 claims side by side, and you will each have a few minutes to write down any observations that arise from reading your peers’ responses next to yours. Where your readings of the book diverge is where discussion starts — divergence is material to explore, not an indication that someone made an error of interpretation. The Discussion Leader’s agenda structures the rest of the hour, the Skeptic and Connector give the discussion its friction and its memory, and the Practitioner keeps us honest about stakes. Nothing you write is filed away unread; all of it does work in the room.
Save everything: your Part 1 claims and the Connector work in particular will be important as you develop your course précis.

title: Session Notes & Discussion Roles
text:
Logistics and grading

Length: 300–450 words total (200–300 core + 100–150 role). The word limits are real and I will enforce them. Being able to distill your thoughts is part of the skill you are developing through this assignment.
Due: on paper at the start of class. Late notes receive no credit (the class needs them before discussion).
Grading: credit/no-credit. Roughly 21 sessions require notes; your best 18 count, so you can miss or fumble a few without a grade penalty.
Async week (Nov 16): the structured discussion of Poor Economics chapters 8–10 uses the Part 1 template only, posted to a Canvas discussion board — initial post by Mon Nov 16 at COB, responses to your colleagues by Wed Nov 18 at COB. No role sections that week. This discussion counts toward your participation grade, not toward the session-notes best-18.
AI policy: session notes must be written in your own words, without generative AI — they are your thinking made visible, and the gap between what you wrote and what you can say in the room is immediately obvious. See the syllabus.

title: Global Development
text:
About This Course
I-522 is a core graduate course for the Masters of International Studies and a core requirement for the Global Development, Environment, and Sustainability concentration of the Masters of International Affairs. We take on large questions: Why are some countries poor while others are not? What theories and approaches explain this divergence? What are the empirical regularities — the drivers and the consequences — of rising standards of living? We examine the political, economic, social, and cultural forces shaping development outcomes, and we consider the roles of geography, institutions, markets, states, international organizations, and domestic governance along the way.
This is a seminar; lecture is minimal. The course works through sustained discussion of six books and a set of recent articles, and it depends on every member arriving prepared, every session. In a small seminar, your preparation is not private — it is the raw material the class runs on.

title: Global Development
text:
How the Course Works
Before each session you will write session notes — in which you identify the reading’s central causal claim, the evidence behind it, and one point you are prepared to argue — plus a short section from your rotating weekly discussion role: Discussion Leader, Skeptic, Connector, or Practitioner. Class opens with a very short scene setting lecture by me. Then we will compare our peers’ notes side by side; any divergence will be an important part of class conversation and each student’s discussion role will help structure productive engagement. Across the semester your notes accumulate into a course précis: your own synthetic map of what causes development, refined in a mid-course workshop and finalized at the end of the term.
Two data projects will help develop students’ familiarity and ease of working with data — one macro (how development is measured, and what the measures hide), one micro (how poor households actually earn, spend, borrow, and insure). An individual final project — a policy memo or a synthetic literature review, your choice — is scaffolded across the second half of the course and presented in the final week.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course description
INTL-I 522 Theoretical and Empirical Overview of Global Development (3 cr.) Explores theories and approaches of global development as well as the political, economic, social, and cultural forces shaping global development outcomes. Considers the role of geography, institutions, global markets and trade, civil society, and historical forces in exploration of the causes and consequences of development.
I-522 is a core graduate course for the Masters of International Studies and a core requirement for the Global Development, Environment, and Sustainability concentration of the Masters of International Affairs. We take on large questions: Why are some countries poor while others are not? What are the principal theories and approaches that explain this divergence? What are the empirical regularities — drivers and consequences — of increased standards of living? We work through six books and a set of recent articles that together trace the field’s central debates, from the meaning and measurement of development itself, through the historical origins of modern growth, the role of the state in industrial transformation, the political economy of Africa’s development, the international institutions that discipline poor-country policy, and the micro-level economics of poverty — ending with the newest frontier: what AI may mean for development. There are no graduate-level prerequisites for this class.

title: Syllabus
text:
Aims & outcomes
By the end of this course you will be able to:

Explain and critically compare the major theoretical approaches to global development — capabilities, institutionalist, structuralist, and experimental — and identify what each takes to be the binding constraint on development.
Evaluate the empirical evidence behind competing causal claims about development, including the strengths and limits of cross-country, historical, and experimental research designs.
Analyze how development is measured, what different measures capture and conceal, and how measurement choices shape policy — at both macro and household levels, using real data.
Assess the role of international institutions, markets, and geopolitics in enabling and constraining development strategies.
Construct your own synthetic causal map of development — the course précis — and defend it.
Produce professional-genre analysis: a policy memo or synthetic literature review, developed through structured milestones and presented to peers.

title: Syllabus
text:
How this course works
This is a graduate seminar — lecture is minimal. The course runs on sustained discussion of shared texts, and in a small seminar every member’s preparation is essential. You are in charge of your learning, not me.

 Before class — session notes with rotating roles
For every reading-bearing session you submit a two-part note: a core analysis (the reading’s central causal claim, the evidence and whether it convinces you, and one point you are prepared to argue) plus a short section written from your rotating weekly role — Discussion Leader, Skeptic, Connector, or Practitioner. Full instructions: Session Notes & Discussion Roles.


 In class — discussion
We open most sessions by putting the session notes side by side; where they diverge is where discussion starts. I will at times provide structured overviews, but the work of the course happens in the conversation.

To prepare, organize your reading notes around these questions: What is the research puzzle? Why does it matter — what gap or inconsistency does it engage? What answer does the author propose, and on what assumptions? How would we know if the author were wrong — what evidence and methodology support the claim? Is the argument convincing, and if not, what would make it more so?

title: Syllabus
text:
Course policies

Intellectual diversity
Development is a field of live disagreement — about what causes growth, what states should do, and what rich countries owe poor ones. Course materials present a variety of arguments, and the seminar is designed for thoughtful, reasoned debate. Four rules help:

Frame disagreements as debates rather than conflicts.
Argue as if you are right, but listen as if you are wrong.
Make the most respectful interpretation of the other person’s perspective.
Acknowledge where you agree with others and what you’ve learned from peers with whom you differ.



Generative AI policy
Generative AI tools are now part of research and policy work, and you may use them in this course — within limits, under your supervision, and with full disclosure.

As a research tool. You may use AI to help you locate literature, explore data, summarize material, and test your understanding of the readings. You are responsible for verifying everything an AI tells you against the actual sources. These tools fabricate citations and misstate findings with complete confidence; an invented source or a wrong claim in your work is your error, not the tool’s.
As a writing aid — supervised and heavily revised. You may use AI to help with some of your writing. Any AI-assisted text must be heavily edited and revised by you before it appears in your work. You are responsible for the precision of your prose and for keeping the common markers of AI writing from overwhelming it: “it’s not X, it’s Y” constructions, overconfident assertion, strange word choices, and a generic voice that is not your own. If a passage reads like a chatbot wrote it, you have not finished the assignment.
Disclosure, always. Every submission in which you used AI in any way — for research, data work, or writing — must include a brief AI-use note stating which tools you used and for what. Undisclosed AI use is academic misconduct and will be handled under the Code of Student Rights, Responsibilities, and Conduct.
The exception: session notes. Session notes must be written entirely in your own words, without generative AI. They are your discussion preparation — your thinking made visible — and the gap between what you wrote and what you can say in the room is immediately obvious.

If you are ever unsure whether a particular use is permitted, ask first.


Accommodations for religious observances
IU respects the right of all students to observe their religion. If you require accommodations for a religious observance, submit a request by the end of the second week (a separate request per absence). I will approve these provided they’re filed within the first two weeks, and you’ll have an opportunity to make up missed work.


Email & office hours
Reserve email for clarifying questions or scheduling; office hours are for substantive questions and grade discussions. I try to respond within one business day. Office hours are also a chance for me to get to know you — which works to your advantage (I write much better recommendation letters for students I know). Arrive with specific questions.


Re-grading requests
After graded material is returned, I maintain a 48-hour reflection period before discussing grades. When I re-examine work with fresh eyes, I reserve the right to assign a grade lower than the original if appropriate.


Honor code
As an IU student you are expected to adhere to the Code of Student Rights, Responsibilities, and Conduct. Submitting work with your name on it signifies it is yours unless otherwise cited. Suspected violations are handled per University policy and reported to the Dean of Students.

title: Assignments
text:
Grade weights and policies are listed on the Syllabus; this page describes each assignment in working detail. Due dates also appear on the Schedule, which is authoritative.

 Participation — 25%

Every session · Week-13 async discussion included

This seminar runs on discussion, and with a small group every voice is required for the course to work. Participation credit reflects prepared, substantive engagement: advancing an argument, testing someone else’s, connecting the current book to earlier frameworks, and building on — rather than past — your colleagues’ contributions. Attendance is necessary but not sufficient. The asynchronous structured discussion of Poor Economics chs. 8–10 (week of Nov 16) counts here.


 Session Notes & Discussion Roles — 20%

Before each reading-bearing class · credit/no-credit · best 18 count

Before every class with assigned reading, bring five printed copies of a two-part note (300–450 words total) to hand in at the start of class:

The core (200–300 words, everyone). The reading’s central causal claim about development; the evidence and whether it convinces you; one point you are prepared to argue in class.
Your role (100–150 words). Each week you hold one of four rotating roles, and your note adds a short section written from that role’s perspective: Discussion Leader (writes the session’s agenda — the 3–5 questions actually worth our discussion time — and steers discussion in class), Skeptic (identifies the weakest link in the causal chain and makes the strongest counterargument), Connector (ties the reading to earlier books and the running causal map), or Practitioner (translates the argument into implications for a government, IO, NGO, or firm).

Notes are due before class and graded credit/no-credit; roughly 21 sessions carry notes and your best 18 count, so there is slack built in. We open most sessions by putting the four core claims side by side — where they diverge is where discussion starts — and the roles give the hour its structure, friction, memory, and stakes. Roles rotate weekly, so you cycle through all four about every four weeks. Save your notes: they are the raw material for your course précis.
Full instructions, role descriptions, and rotation details: Session Notes & Discussion Roles.


 Data Project 1: Measuring Development — 7.5%

Assigned Mon Aug 31 · Due Fri Sep 4, COB (Canvas) · in-class debrief Sep 9

How development is measured shapes what development means. Choose a region and three focus countries, investigate them through at least three distinct measures of development, chart the trends, and analyze what each measure captures, what it hides, and where the measures disagree — and why. Deliverable: a 3–4 page data brief with data appendix, presented at the Sep 9 debrief (which replaces our cancelled Sep 2 meeting).
Generative AI may assist with data wrangling and visualization, with disclosure (see the AI policy on the Syllabus); the analysis and interpretation must be yours.
Full instructions, sources, and the evaluation rubric: Data Projects.


 Data Project 2: The Economic Lives of the Poor — 7.5%

Assigned week of Nov 16 · Due Fri Nov 20, COB (Canvas) · in-class debrief Nov 30

The micro-level counterpart to Project 1, keyed to Poor Economics. Using household-level data (DHS, LSMS, Global Findex, or a J-PAL evaluation, among others), profile how poor households in one of your Project 1 countries earn, spend, borrow, and insure. Connect what you find to Banerjee and Duflo’s evidence — and to the macro measures from Project 1: what does the micro view reveal that your aggregates concealed? Same format and AI-disclosure terms as Project 1. Debrief in class Mon Nov 30.
Full instructions, sources, and the evaluation rubric: Data Projects.


 Course Précis — 10%

Workshopped Mon Oct 5 · Final version due Mon Dec 14

Across the semester you will build a synthetic overview of the course’s key concepts — in words and figures, with particular attention to causal chains: what causes development, through what mechanisms, on what evidence. Your session notes feed it directly, and the shared causal map we develop in class informs each student’s individual document. We workshop the précis on Oct 5, mapping the causal arguments of Sen, Koyama & Rubin, and Evans against each other, and we return to it as each new book complicates the map. The final version should be a document you can take with you — a high-quality summary of what this course taught you about how development works.
Full instructions, required components, and evaluation criteria: Course Précis.


 Final Project — 30%

Individual · milestones Oct 9 → Nov 6 → Nov 30 → Dec 7 · Final version due Wed Dec 16

Choose one of two genres:

Policy memo — max 4 pages single-spaced plus appendices, addressed to a government, international organization, or agency of your choice, analyzing one development challenge and proposing a response. Do not let the short length fool you: memos must be impeccably researched, and space is the constraint that forces judgment.
Synthetic literature review — 10–15 pages single-spaced: an authoritative overview of the concepts, findings, and debates around one development question, an evaluation of the evidence used to adjudicate theoretical claims, and suggestions for where the literature should go. Especially useful if you are considering doctoral study.

title: Final Project
text: The final project is where you take ownership of one development question and produce something in a professional genre — the kind of document you may write in your career. It is an individual project, developed across the second half of the semester through a series of milestones, presented to the class in our final week, and revised before final submission. This page provides detailed instructions; the assignments page has the summary and the syllabus has grade weights and policies.

title: Final Project
text:
Choosing your genre
You will choose one of two genres. Both are legitimate professional forms, and the right choice depends on your interests and career goals. I encourage you to come to office hours before the topic memo is due to talk through your options.

 Option 1 — Policy memo
A memo of no more than 4 pages, single-spaced (plus appendices), addressed to a specific government agency, international organization, or NGO of your choice. Your memo will analyze one development challenge and propose a course of action. Do not let the short length fool you: memos must be impeccably researched, and it will be hard to cover everything you need in that little space. The discipline of deciding what to leave out is a large part of what this genre teaches. This option will help you develop the capacity to translate research into potential policy strategies.


 Option 2 — Synthetic literature review
A review of 10–15 pages, single-spaced, providing an authoritative overview of the main concepts, findings, and debates around one question of development. This is a deep dive into an issue we covered briefly in class, or one we did not cover at all. Your review should organize the literature around its debates rather than marching through papers one at a time, evaluate the kinds of evidence scholars use to assess theoretical claims, and offer suggestions for how the literature could move forward. This option is especially useful if you are considering a PhD or a more research-oriented (rather than policy or practitioner) trajectory.

title: Final Project
text:
What makes a strong project
Whichever genre you choose, I will be looking for the same underlying qualities we practice all semester in session notes: a precisely stated causal claim, intellectually honest engagement with the evidence for and against it (rather than relying on motivated reasoning), and awareness of what the argument implies for practice. Strong projects take a position. A memo that lists considerations without recommending anything, or a literature review that summarizes extant research without adjudicating persistent debates in the field, has not finished the analytic work.
Your topic should connect to the themes of this course, but it does not need to come from the assigned readings. If you are unsure whether a topic will work, ask early.

title: Final Project
text:
Evaluation
Policy memos are evaluated on the clarity and specificity of the recommendation, the quality of the research behind it, the extent to which costs and counterarguments are adequately addressed, and the professionalism of the writing — your addressee should be able to act on this document.
Literature reviews are evaluated on coverage of the relevant scholarship, the quality of the synthesis (debates and adjudication, not summary), the sophistication of the evidence evaluation, and the usefulness of the suggested paths forward for future research.
Both genres are evaluated on writing as well as content. Impeccable prose, accurate citation, and clean presentation are part of the assignment. People will pay attention to what you say when you can communicate your thoughts clearly, succinctly, and in a manner that is enjoyable to read.

title: Final Project
text:
Policies
The course generative AI policy applies to every milestone: you may use AI as a research tool and, with heavy editing and revision under your supervision, as a writing aid — but every use must be disclosed in a brief AI-use note submitted with the milestone, and the argument, the analysis, and the final prose are your responsibility. Remember that both genres are evaluated on the quality of the writing; prose that is heavily reliant on AI is usually not precise enough for prime time.
The late-work policy on the syllabus applies to every milestone; because each milestone feeds the next, falling behind compounds quickly. Talk to me early if you are struggling.

title: Data Projects
text:
You will complete two data projects during this semester — one at the macro and one at the micro level.
In the first, you look at development from above — the aggregate measures that governments, international organizations, and scholars use to say whether a country is developing.
In the second, you look from below — household-level data on how poor families actually earn, spend, borrow, and manage risk.
These projects, then, function in part to help us address a question of levels in development. How do individual behaviors aggregate to economy-wide progress on a range of development measures? Is development an individualistic/household project or a social one?
These are data literacy projects, not statistics projects. I am not asking you to run regressions, and you do not need any statistical training beyond careful reading of charts and tables. The skills being practiced here are the ones you will use constantly in policy careers: finding credible data, understanding what a measure actually captures, presenting numbers in an unbiased way, and drawing conclusions that the data can support.

title: Data Projects
text:
Data Project 1 — Measuring Development

Assigned Mon Aug 31 · Due Friday Sep 4 by COB, on Canvas · 7.5%

How development is measured shapes what development means — this is one of Sen’s central points, and this project helps you see this in practice by comparing different measures of development.

The task

Choose a region (Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Latin America, Southeast Asia, MENA, or Central Asia), and within it, three focus countries with different development trajectories. Each student should take a different region — coordinate on the sign-up sheet posted on Canvas.
Choose at least three distinct measures of development. At least one must be income-based (GDP per capita, ideally PPP-adjusted; or the international poverty headcount) and at least one must be non-income or composite (HDI, the Multidimensional Poverty Index, inequality-adjusted HDI, life expectancy, mean years of schooling). The resources page lists where you can find each of these data sources.
Chart the trends. For each measure, show how your focus countries have moved over the longest sensible window the data allow (for GDP per capita that may be 60 years; for the MPI it may be 15 — and that difference in coverage is itself worth discussing). Every figure needs labeled axes, units, years, and a source line.
Analyze what the measures capture and hide. Where do your measures agree about which country is doing well, and where do they disagree? What does each measure assume development is? What would Sen say about each? Which countries look different depending on the yardstick — and why, concretely?
Take a position. Close with a short recommendation: if you could report only one of your measures to a minister or country director to track this region’s progress, which would you choose, and what would you be knowingly giving up?



The deliverable
A data brief of 3–4 pages (single-spaced, figures included in the page count), written for an intelligent professional reader, plus a data appendix (not counted in the page limit) listing every series you used: indicator name, source, years covered, and any gaps or oddities you encountered. Submit as a PDF on Canvas by COB Sept 4, and come to class on Sept 9 ready to present your findings in about five minutes at the debrief — expect questions about why the measures disagree.

title: Data Projects
section: Data Project 2 — The Economic Lives of the Poor
text:
Data Project 2 — The Economic Lives of the Poor

Assigned week of Nov 16 · Due Fri Nov 20, COB; on Canvas · presented at the Nov 30 debrief · 7.5%

Banerjee and Duflo’s Poor Economics emphasizes a different level of analysis: instead of asking how poor countries behave, they ask how poor households behave. This project has you explore this microlevel of analysis with real household data — and then confront what you find with the macroeconomic picture you built in Project 1.

The task

Choose one country — ideally, one of your three focus countries from Project 1, so the macro–micro comparison is direct. (If you switch countries, say why in the brief.)
Build a portrait of poor households’ economic lives in that country, covering three of these five domains, with at least six indicators total:

Earning: income sources, informality, agricultural vs. non-farm work
Spending: budget shares, food vs. non-food, spending that surprises you
Financial lives: saving, borrowing, account ownership (Global Findex is built for this)
Risk: health shocks, insurance coverage, coping strategies
Investing in the future: education and health spending, school enrollment and attainment

Use household-level sources. DHS STATcompiler, Global Findex, LSMS tables, IPUMS tabulations, or a J-PAL evaluation’s published data — the resources page links each. These tools give you tabulated indicators; you do not need to analyze or manipulate raw survey microdata (though you may).
Confront the two levels. Where does the household view confirm what Banerjee and Duflo report, and where does your country diverge from their composite picture of “the poor”? Most importantly: what does the micro view reveal that your Project 1 aggregates concealed — and is there anything the aggregates showed that the household data cannot?



The deliverable
Same format as Project 1: a 3–4 page data brief with a data appendix, submitted as a PDF on Canvas by Friday, Nov 20 at COB, and a roughly five-minute presentation at the Nov 30 debrief.

title: Data Projects
section: How I will evaluate both projects
text:
How I will evaluate both projects








Criterion
Weight
What I am looking for




Data handling & documentation
25%
Appropriate sources; correct units and comparisons; a complete, honest data appendix; gaps acknowledged rather than papered over


Figures
25%
Charts that are accurate, labeled, sourced, and readable — a figure should make its point without the caption doing all the work


Interpretation & measurement critique
30%
Analysis that goes beyond describing the lines: what the measures assume, what they hide, where they disagree, and why


Connection & communication
20%
Explicit engagement with course arguments (Sen for Project 1; Banerjee & Duflo for Project 2); clear, precise prose within the page limit



The most common way to lose points on assignments like these is to submit a data dump — many charts, little argument. The second most common way is false precision: treating a poverty rate as exact when the underlying survey has a confidence interval and a five-year gap between rounds. Noticing imprecision is not a weakness of your brief; it is an important skill to develop.
